rules.name: Satisfaction relation seed
rules.input_form: structure M, assignment s, formula phi
preconditions: A formal language, structure, and assignment are fixed
rules.operation: Evaluate a formula semantically inside a structure under the standard satisfaction clauses.
examples: Truth in a structure depends on both interpretation data and variable assignment
counterexamples: Treating formal provability and semantic satisfaction as identical is invalid in general

rules.name: Elementary equivalence seed
rules.input_form: structures M and N in a common language
preconditions: The structures are interpreted in the same first-order language
rules.operation: Identify structures that satisfy exactly the same first-order sentences.
examples: Nonisomorphic structures can still be elementarily equivalent
counterexamples: Isomorphism is stronger than elementary equivalence, so replacing one by the other is invalid

rules.name: Turing computability seed
rules.input_form: function with algorithmic specification
preconditions: A standard Turing-machine model and input-output convention are fixed
rules.operation: Classify a function as computable by existence of a halting correct machine procedure.
examples: Effective finite-step symbolic procedures are modeled by Turing-computable functions in the standard setting
counterexamples: Describing a function informally without a halting effective procedure is insufficient

rules.name: Decidability seed
rules.input_form: language of encoded inputs
rules.output_form: decidable iff some total correct decision machine exists
preconditions: An encoding and machine model are fixed
rules.operation: Recognize decidability by existence of a total halting decision procedure.
examples: Total halting behavior distinguishes decision procedures from partial recognizers
counterexamples: Semidecidability alone is insufficient for decidability

rules.name: Simply typed lambda judgment seed
rules.input_form: Gamma |- t : T
preconditions: A typing context and simply typed lambda calculus are fixed
rules.operation: Assign a type to a term through a valid typing derivation.
examples: Typing rules constrain application and abstraction by domain-codomain compatibility
counterexamples: Applying a nonfunction term as though it had an arrow type is invalid

rules.name: Curry-Howard bridge seed
rules.input_form: proposition and proof system with typed terms
preconditions: A compatible typed proof-term system is fixed
rules.operation: Relate propositions to types and proofs to terms under Curry-Howard.
examples: Implication behaves like a function type under the propositions-as-types reading
counterexamples: Treating every semantic truth automatically as a proof term is invalid

rules.name: Compactness seed
rules.input_form: set of first-order sentences
preconditions: A first-order language and standard semantic setting are fixed
rules.operation: Pass from satisfiability of every finite fragment to satisfiability of the full theory.
examples: Global model existence can be forced through consistent finite fragments rather than by constructing the full model directly
counterexamples: Inferring compactness-style behavior for stronger logics without qualification is invalid

rules.name: Lowenheim-Skolem seed
rules.input_form: first-order theory with an infinite model
rules.output_form: existence of models at controlled infinite cardinalities
preconditions: A first-order theory and infinite-model hypothesis are fixed
rules.operation: Transfer infinite model existence across standard Löwenheim-Skolem cardinality regimes.
examples: First-order syntax cannot pin down one unique infinite size merely by categorical intent
counterexamples: Assuming one infinite model cardinality forces uniqueness across all first-order models is invalid

rules.name: Universal machine seed
rules.input_form: encoded machine and encoded input
preconditions: A standard encoding of machines and inputs is fixed
rules.operation: Simulate any encoded machine-input pair on one universal Turing machine.
examples: Machine descriptions can themselves be treated as inputs to a single universal simulator
counterexamples: A machine specialized to one finite task family is not automatically universal

rules.name: Many-one reduction seed
rules.input_form: pair of decision problems with a computable translation
preconditions: A computable encoding map between the problems is fixed
rules.operation: Transfer decision complexity by computable many-one reduction.
examples: Hardness is transferred by effective encoding rather than by verbal similarity of problems
counterexamples: An informal analogy between problems with no computable reduction map is invalid

rules.name: Halting undecidability seed
rules.input_form: encoded machine-input pair
preconditions: A universal machine encoding and total-decision interpretation are fixed
rules.operation: Reject existence of a total decision procedure for the general halting problem.
examples: Universal simulation power also creates undecidable boundary problems for total algorithmic prediction
counterexamples: Solving halting only for one restricted machine family does not refute general undecidability

rules.name: Dependent type family seed
rules.input_form: type expression indexed by term data
preconditions: A dependent type theory with term-indexed families is fixed
rules.operation: Allow types to vary with terms in indexed families.
examples: Vectors indexed by length encode both data and size constraints in one typed object
counterexamples: Treating every simply typed system as already dependent is invalid

rules.name: Normalization seed
rules.input_form: well-typed lambda term under a normalizing reduction discipline
preconditions: A typed reduction system with normalization guarantees is fixed
rules.operation: Reduce well-typed terms to normal form through admissible computation steps.
examples: Computation in proof-term systems can be viewed as normalization rather than arbitrary term rewriting
counterexamples: Allowing unrestricted self-application destroys the standard normalization guarantee

rules.name: Canonical form normalization expansion
rules.input_form: raw expression E
preconditions: Auto-expansion rule requires explicit domain assumptions and validation metadata
rules.operation: Rewrite expressions into a canonical form that preserves the active equivalence relation.
examples: x + y and y + x map to a shared canonical additive form in commutative settings
counterexamples: Applying canonicalization rules outside their preconditions is invalid
common_errors: Using auto-generated rules without confirming domain-specific assumptions
